narrator: A developer who puts the plugin on clients' sites, walking a colleague through it: calm, plain and quietly upbeat. Every step he names is one the walkthrough (tests/e2e/developer/install.developer.mjs) performs on a WordPress the plugin was never installed on (run-docker.cmd fresh).

intro.en: This is Viglet Turing Search, an open source plugin for WordPress and WooCommerce. In the next few minutes I'll put it on a WordPress shop that has never had it, connect it to Viglet Turing, index the catalog, and show what the shop and its owner get from it.

card.en: It installs like any other plugin. Under Plugins, Add New, I upload the release zip and install it. The same package also works from Composer.

result.en: Activated. It adds one menu, Viglet Turing Search, and everything it does lives under it: settings, setup, fields, health, tuning and insights.

card.en: The Setup page asks for four things: the address of your Turing, an API key created in Turing, the name of the Semantic Navigation site, and the language the content is written in.

result.en: [pleased] It tests every step on the way: the address, the network, Turing itself, the key, and the site. This site didn't exist yet, so one click created it, with the fields the plugin needs.

card.en: By default it indexes posts and pages. This one is a shop, so under Settings, Indexing, I turn on products as well.

result.en: Saved. Categories, tags and custom fields can go in the same way, and the Fields page maps each content type's fields.

card.en: Back on Setup, the first index sends every published item of those types, in batches, with its progress on screen.

result.en: Done. The whole catalog and its guides are in Viglet Turing. From now on, a new or edited post is sent on its own, in the background.

card.en: Over on the storefront, the search block now asks Viglet Turing. I'll type a plain search.

result.en: [upbeat] Results, with filters built from the shop's own fields: category, stock, colour, size and price. Nobody had to configure those by hand.

card.en: And the owner sees what visitors look for, under Insights.

result.en: The search I just made is already counted. Top searches, searches that found nothing, and results nobody opened: each one tells the shop what to fix next.

outro.en: That's the whole setup: a zip, a key and one index. The code is on GitHub, the documentation is on the Viglet site, and the demo store runs right in your browser, with nothing to install.
